context: Current closing price of Southwest Airlines (LUV): $48.58 USD as of 2026-07-10.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was a recent observed price or index level near $48–49. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of $48.75 is essentially anchored to the last known price with only marginal drift, reflecting the tendency of financial assets to exhibit near-random-walk behavior over very short periods. The slight upward tilt at one week ($49.10) and one month ($49.80) incorporates a small positive drift assumption, consistent with a long-run equity risk premium or modest bullish momentum, while acknowledging that mean reversion and noise will dominate over these relatively short windows.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect typical realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly $46.80 to $50.70 implies an annualized volatility in the neighborhood of 20–25%, which is a reasonable baseline for a broad equity instrument or moderately volatile asset. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, the intervals widen substantially — from about $7 wide at one week to over $15 wide at one month — reflecting the compounding of daily uncertainty. This is a standard feature of probabilistic forecasting where uncertainty grows with time, and no strong mean-reverting anchor was assumed strong enough to compress longer-horizon intervals.

Several structural sources of uncertainty shaped these intervals beyond pure statistical volatility. Macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, geopolitical developments, and shifts in market liquidity can all introduce discontinuous jumps that a smooth volatility model would underweight. At the one-month horizon in particular, the interval may still be too narrow if there is an upcoming scheduled event such as a Federal Reserve meeting, earnings season, or major economic report that could shift the price regime materially.

Tail risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a sudden credit event or financial contagion shock on the downside, or an unexpected dovish policy pivot or strong economic surprise on the upside. Black swan events — geopolitical escalation, a liquidity crisis, or an abrupt sentiment shift — are by definition underweighted in historically calibrated volatility estimates. These are precisely the scenarios where stated 90% intervals fail, and a prudent user of these forecasts should treat the tails as fatter than the symmetric intervals imply.
